segments.text: His leg is broken. He's hanging off a cliff, in the dark, in a storm. The only thing holding him is a rope. And at the other end of it is his climbing partner. Then the rope goes slack.
Somebody cut that. And nobody comes back from a drop like this one. No chance. Let's go look.

June, {1985|nineteen eighty-five}. The Andes of Peru. Two British climbers, Joe Simpson and Simon Yates, both in their twenties, are looking up at a mountain called Siula Grande. Nobody has ever climbed its west face.
A third man, Richard Hawking, stays behind at base camp. He is not a climber. Smart man.
It takes them three days. On the third, they are standing on the summit. The first people ever to come up that face.
But the top is only halfway. They start down the north ridge. And that night, the stove burns the last of their gas. No gas means no melting snow. No melting snow means nothing to drink.
The next morning, Simpson falls from an ice cliff on the ridge, and lands badly. His right leg is broken at the knee.
Up here, nobody is coming to help. There are two of them, one good pair of legs, and nearly three thousand feet of mountain still below.
So Yates makes a plan. He knots their two ropes into one, three hundred feet long. He digs himself a seat in the snow. And he lowers his partner down the mountain, one rope at a time.
It works. Lower after lower, into the dark, into a storm. I stopped making jokes about then.
Then Yates lowers him over the edge of a cliff that neither of them can see. Simpson is hanging in space. His hands are frostbitten. He cannot climb the rope.
Up on the slope, Yates cannot see him. All he has is the weight. He holds it for more than an hour. And the whole time, the seat under him is crumbling.
Now he is being pulled off the mountain himself. In his rucksack, there is a knife. He cuts the rope.

Yates spends the night in a hole in the snow. In the morning he climbs down past the cliff, and finds a crevasse at the foot of it. There is no sign of his friend. He is sure Simpson is dead. He walks back to camp alone.
But here is what he could not see. Simpson fell into that crevasse, and landed on a ledge inside it. Alive.
He can't climb out. The ice overhangs, and his leg is useless.
So he does the one thing left. He lowers himself deeper, into the dark, not knowing if the rope will reach anything at all.
Down there, a slope of snow leads up to a hole, and daylight.
He drags himself out onto the glacier. Camp is miles away. He has no food, and almost no water. So he crawls. Across the ice. Then hopping, and falling, through the boulders below it. For three days.
On the last night, he reaches camp. Yates and Hawking were due to leave in a few hours. A few hours more, and there would have been nobody there.

It takes two days by mule to get him out of the mountains, and then a hospital in Lima. He has lost about a third of his body weight. His leg needs six operations. Two years later, he is climbing again.

Back home, some climbers blame Yates. The man who cut the rope. Simpson won't have it. He says he would have done exactly the same. And he writes a book, partly to set the record straight. He calls it Touching the Void.
And here is the part that got me. Both men have said the same thing since. Cutting the rope is what saved them both.
I came up here to find the villain of this story. There isn't one. One man held on for as long as he could. The other one crawled home. I was wrong. Case closed.
